strengths: The proposed method/framework demonstrated good empirical performance on the studied datasets across many different downstream tasks.
The experiments were performed on two datasets.
The models have been compared to multiple baselines.
They propose the use of a unified framework called LEA, that tackles both fMRI decoding and encoding. This is a step forward in the field, which often treats these tasks separately.
They also introduce an innovative ROI-induced embedding layer that addresses the issue of varying dimensions in fMRI signals.
Their qualitative results seem largely sound.
weaknesses: The presentation of the paper isn’t clear, which not only posts challenge to its readability but also undermines its methodological contributions.

Weird terminology and unclear contributions. Encoding typically refer to extracting meaningful representation from the input data; and decoding typically refer to generating realistic data from meaningful representations. In this paper, however, the first paragraph and the related work section seems to define ‘decoding’ as using fMRI to generate images; and ‘encoding’ as generating fMRI from images. However, in later paragraphs, the authors continue to use the original definition of encoding and decoding by referring MAE as “encoder-decoder architecture training”. Thus, the major contribution of the work “simultaneously tackling the tasks of fMRI decoding and encoding” reads unclear based on the not-clearly defined terminology.

Unclear math definitions. For example, Equation 1 shows the loss for the model training. What are the parameters trained and why they are not inside the equations? What are the architecture of the referred layers, e.g. RoI Project layer? For the latent embedding alignment, how is the linear model trained? It is challenging to decipher the correctness of the approach without such methodological details.

Grammar issues. e.g. “Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that LEA not only exhibits superiority in the domains of fMRI decoding and encoding.” “the totally amount of training fMRI data”.

Lack of ablation experiments. The work lack methodological insights if it is unclear which part of the model is taking an effect. Is the method better because the alignment is through a linear model regression? Is the backbone architecture better or more complex (contains more parameters)? Is the RoI module taking an effect? The Table 6 in appendix (the only ablation I found through the text) reveals very little information.

Unclear experimental details. What are the backbone architecture of the baselines? Are the comparison fair in terms of the amount of parameters? The authors should justify as such by providing necessary details.

Overall, I believe the presented paper lacks necessary details in the introduction section; methodology section; as well as the experimental results section. It is challenging to validate the effectiveness and novelty of the proposed approach without such details.

Using the test subset of the dataset via reconstruction task creates data leakage; the test set should only be used for final performance reporting, not for any part of the experiments, hyperparameter tuning, or checkpoint selection. No validation set or cross‑validation details were provided.

It is not clear whether the data were split subject‑wise; if not, this creates additional data leakage. A leave‑one‑subject‑out strategy and careful handling of fMRI time‑series versus image pairing are recommended to avoid leakage.

Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4 do not show variability of the approaches; multiple runs, statistical measures (STD, SE, IQR) and statistical significance testing with correction for multiple comparisons are needed.

Missing related work: MindEye (Scotti et al., 2023) which also uses the NSD dataset and contrastive loss for alignment; the authors should discuss and potentially provide ablations for such strategies.

The authors claim that “Our method begins by side‑stepping the necessity for paired image‑fMRI data”, but then relax it to “without the need for extensive paired training data”, causing ambiguity about the data requirements.

The authors claim that encoder‑decoder architectures can be trained via self‑supervised learning techniques, but they only demonstrate a basic auto‑encoder with a single token bottleneck, not the claimed self‑supervised methods.
It is unclear how the alignment between the fMRI latent space and the image latent space is performed; Section 3.3 provides very few details.

Zero‑shot classification of brain activations relies on CLIP, which differs from the SVM‑based zero‑shot results reported for baselines such as CADA‑VAE; this discrepancy should be clarified in the paper.
The overall approach appears similar to BrainCLIP, with the only novelty being the ROI‑level transformer auto‑encoder, which may not be sufficiently novel.
Figure 2 is misleading because it is unclear whether the data are fMRI time‑series or fMRI betas, and presenting the ROI time‑series as a continuous series is potentially inaccurate.
Table 2 reports Pearson R values greater than 1, which is impossible; Pearson R is also an unusual metric for evaluating encoding models, where explained variance is more common [1].
The paper lacks visualizations of cortical surface activations and does not show how R or explained variance varies across ROIs, making it hard to assess model performance spatially.
There are many small typos and oddly phrased sentences throughout the paper, making it difficult to read.
Various minor typographical errors throughout the manuscript (e.g., “is crucial to understand” → “is crucial to understanding”, “is still challenge” → “is still challenging”, etc.).
Serious typographical errors in the abstract and other sections (e.g., “in recovering brain recordings by generating images conditioned on fMRI signals” is unclear), further harming readability.
